bull_case: Nu combines a low-cost digital operating model, proprietary data/AI and mobile distribution to replace high-friction Latin American banking while expanding from cards into deposits, lending, investments and SME services.
bear_case: The original disruption may mature into ordinary banking competition. Incumbents and other fintechs can match digital interfaces, while deposit pricing, regulation and credit losses can erode the cost advantage.
thesis: Nu remains a scaled disruptive platform rather than a pilot-stage fintech. The digital model serves well over 100M customers at roughly $0.8 monthly cost-to-serve, while deposits and credit products deepen primary banking relationships. Adoption is mainstream. The strongest evidence is cost/distribution structure and continued share gains; the limiting factor is that banking products can be copied and regulatory/credit constraints eventually make parts of the model look more like conventional banking.

evidence.claim: Nu reported monthly average cost to serve per active customer of about $0.8 in 2025 while serving 131M customers, demonstrating a very low-cost digital service model at scale.
Q2 2026 customers reached 138.9M and monthly activity rate 83.5%, with Brazil above 86%.
Deposits reached $45.3B in Q2 2026; the 20-F states the retail deposit franchise has grown steadily and more than covered funding needs.

Nu has monetized multiple adjacent pools beyond the original credit card: deposits, personal/payroll loans, investments, SMEs and premium banking, with Mexico and Colombia adding geographic optionality.
Nu disclosed plans to expand its proprietary transformer-based NuFormer approach into Brazil lending and Mexico credit cards, extending data/AI into underwriting decisions.

counterevidence: Digital banking interfaces are increasingly standard and can be copied by incumbents and other fintechs.
High deposit yields used to acquire customers can narrow the structural cost advantage.
Credit and regulatory capital requirements make scaling more capital intensive than pure software.
Brazil already has high Nu penetration, shifting future disruption toward wallet share and international execution.
unknowns: Independent full-cycle cost advantage versus the most efficient incumbent banks.
How much NuFormer improves risk-adjusted credit returns after deployment.
Long-run profitability of Mexico and Colombia after full product breadth.
falsifiers: Cost-to-serve rises materially as product complexity increases without offsetting monetization.
Activity and primary-bank share stop increasing despite customer growth.
International markets require sustained deposit subsidies without converging unit economics.

key_kpis.name: International unit economics
key_kpis.threshold: Mexico/Colombia progress toward self-funded profitable growth

next_checks: Track NuFormer underwriting deployment and loss outcomes.
Track Mexico bank launch economics and deposit cost.
Compare cost-to-serve and activity with leading regional competitors.

subscores.rationale: Nu's low-cost digital distribution and roughly $0.8 monthly service cost structurally change banking convenience and cost, but a universal 10x economic advantage versus all efficient banks is not established.
Nearly 139M customers, >83% monthly activity and large deposits/credit balances demonstrate mainstream adoption at regional scale.
Three or more adjacent value pools are already monetized—deposits, lending, investments/SME/premium services—and Nu is helping define the digital primary-bank model across its core markets.

uncertainties.rationale: The low-cost model is directly evidenced; comparative full-cycle profitability versus efficient banks is less standardized.
Adoption is clear; future monetization quality is the greater uncertainty.
Well-capitalized banks and fintechs can copy individual products even if the full ecosystem is harder to replicate.
